description: How can we know what traditions must be respected and which ones should be changed? All societies must contend with the challenges posed by the rise of new ideologies, philosophies, and belief systems. But when these new ideas threaten the established order, how leaders respond can mean the difference between life and death. This course focuses on the struggles of two political communities at critical junctures in their histories -- imperial Ming China and England under Henry VIII. Over the course of the semester, we will engage in extensive role-playing games where you assume the roles of important historical political figures and factions and use writing and speaking to persuade other students to agree with your position. In this way, we will explore the philosophical and moral dimensions of autocratic power and elitism in leadership and decision-making to better understand some of the critical issues facing society today. Specifically, we will examine Ming China in 1587 and the Reformation Parliament in England from 1529 to 1536 in order to compare their debates and experiences wrestling with questions like the following: What is the nature of autocratic power? How do social norms and traditions serve as limits on autocratic power? Does absolute power corrupt absolutely? What is the ideal relationship between the government and the people? What are the ideal characteristics of the ruler? Can immoral means ever justify moral ends?
